claim: Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein that regulates MT structure and function during neuronal development.
source: Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein that regulates MT structure and function during neuronal development and mutations in DCX lead to a spectrum of neurological disorders.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of DCX.

claim: Mutations in DCX lead to a spectrum of neurological disorders.
source: Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule (MT)-associated protein that regulates MT structure and function during neuronal development and mutations in DCX lead to a spectrum of neurological disorders.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: DCX interacts with MTs through its N-terminal domain.
source: We demonstrate that DCX interacts with MTs through its N-terminal domain and induces a lattice-dependent self-association involving the C-terminal structured domain and its disordered tail, in a conformation that favors an open, domain-swapped state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by integrative modeling data.

claim: DCX induces a lattice-dependent self-association involving the C-terminal structured domain and its disordered tail.
source: We demonstrate that DCX interacts with MTs through its N-terminal domain and induces a lattice-dependent self-association involving the C-terminal structured domain and its disordered tail, in a conformation that favors an open, domain-swapped state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by crosslinking and modeling data.

claim: DCX self-association favors an open, domain-swapped state.
source: We demonstrate that DCX interacts with MTs through its N-terminal domain and induces a lattice-dependent self-association involving the C-terminal structured domain and its disordered tail, in a conformation that favors an open, domain-swapped state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by integrative modeling comparing globular and open CDC conformations.

claim: The networked state of DCX can accommodate multiple different attachment points on the MT lattice.
source: The networked state can accommodate multiple different attachment points on the MT lattice, all of which orient the C-terminal tails away from the lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling data showing multiple orientations.

claim: All DCX attachment points on the MT lattice orient the C-terminal tails away from the lattice.
source: The networked state can accommodate multiple different attachment points on the MT lattice, all of which orient the C-terminal tails away from the lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by density maps shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Numerous disease mutations cluster in the C-terminus of DCX.
source: As numerous disease mutations cluster in the C-terminus, and regulatory phosphorylations cluster in its tail, our study shows that lattice-driven self-assembly is an important property of DCX.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced in the introduction.

claim: Regulatory phosphorylations cluster in the C-terminal tail of DCX.
source: As numerous disease mutations cluster in the C-terminus, and regulatory phosphorylations cluster in its tail, our study shows that lattice-driven self-assembly is an important property of DCX.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Tanaka et al., 2004; Graham et al., 2004; Shmueli et al., 2006).

claim: Lattice-driven self-assembly is an important property of DCX.
source: As numerous disease mutations cluster in the C-terminus, and regulatory phosphorylations cluster in its tail, our study shows that lattice-driven self-assembly is an important property of DCX.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: DCX is essential for neuronal migration in embryonic and postnatal brain development.
source: Doublecortin (DCX) is a 40-kDa MAP, essential for neuronal migration in embryonic and postnatal brain development (des Portes et al., 1998a, Gleeson et al., 1998; Francis et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX influences MT rigidity and curvature.
source: DCX influences MT rigidity and curvature and selects for the canonical 13-protofilament geometry that is characteristic of most eukaryotic MTs (Moores et al., 2004; Jean et al., 2012; Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014; Ettinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX selects for the canonical 13-protofilament geometry that is characteristic of most eukaryotic MTs.
source: DCX influences MT rigidity and curvature and selects for the canonical 13-protofilament geometry that is characteristic of most eukaryotic MTs (Moores et al., 2004; Jean et al., 2012; Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014; Ettinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX increases the nucleation rate of MTs.
source: It also increases the nucleation rate and decreases the catastrophe rate (Moores et al., 2006), producing a net stabilization of MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX decreases the catastrophe rate of MTs.
source: It also increases the nucleation rate and decreases the catastrophe rate (Moores et al., 2006), producing a net stabilization of MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX produces a net stabilization of MTs.
source: It also increases the nucleation rate and decreases the catastrophe rate (Moores et al., 2006), producing a net stabilization of MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of DCX's effects on nucleation and catastrophe rates.

claim: Mutations in the doublecortin gene result in lissencephaly ('smooth brain') or subcortical band heterotopia.
source: Mutations in the doublecortin gene result in lissencephaly ('smooth brain') or subcortical band heterotopia, both of which can generate a spectrum of intellectual disabilities and/or epilepsy (des Portes et al., 1998b, Gleeson et al., 1998; des Portes et al., 1998a, Gleeson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lissencephaly and subcortical band heterotopia can generate a spectrum of intellectual disabilities and/or epilepsy.
source: Mutations in the doublecortin gene result in lissencephaly ('smooth brain') or subcortical band heterotopia, both of which can generate a spectrum of intellectual disabilities and/or epilepsy (des Portes et al., 1998b, Gleeson et al., 1998; des Portes et al., 1998a, Gleeson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX mutations impair binding of DCX to MTs.
source: These mutations impair binding of DCX to MTs (Taylor et al., 2000) but the structural basis for this effect remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX consists of a tandem repeat of Doublecortin-like (DC) domains possessing 27% sequence identity.
source: DCX consists of a tandem repeat of Doublecortin-like (DC) domains possessing 27% sequence identity, an N-terminal tail (N-tail), a linker region, and a long Serine/Proline-rich C-terminal tail (C-tail) (Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both of the DC domains and the linker region are necessary for the MT stabilization effect.
source: Both of the DC domains and the linker region are necessary for the MT stabilization effect (Taylor et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2003), whereas the C-terminal DC domain (CDC) (Manka and Moores, 2020) and the C-tail (Moores et al., 2004) help establish the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal DC domain (CDC) helps establish the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
source: Both of the DC domains and the linker region are necessary for the MT stabilization effect (Taylor et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2003), whereas the C-terminal DC domain (CDC) (Manka and Moores, 2020) and the C-tail (Moores et al., 2004) help establish the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-tail helps establish the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
source: Both of the DC domains and the linker region are necessary for the MT stabilization effect (Taylor et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2003), whereas the C-terminal DC domain (CDC) (Manka and Moores, 2020) and the C-tail (Moores et al., 2004) help establish the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-tail is implicated in regulating MT–actin interactions.
source: The C-tail is also implicated in regulating MT–actin interactions (Fu et al., 2013; Jean et al., 2012; Tsukada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Structures are only available for the isolated N-terminal DC domain (NDC) and the CDC.
source: Structures are only available for the isolated N-terminal DC domain (NDC) (Kim et al., 2003; Cierpicki et al., 2006; Burger et al., 2016) and the CDC (Burger et al., 2016; Rufer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: NDC and CDC structures share the same globular ubiquitin-like fold.
source: For the most part, these structures share the same globular ubiquitin-like fold, although the CDC may adopt a substantially opened form (Rufer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The CDC may adopt a substantially opened form.
source: For the most part, these structures share the same globular ubiquitin-like fold, although the CDC may adopt a substantially opened form (Rufer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Disease mutations cluster in both of the structured domains of DCX.
source: Disease mutations cluster in both of the structured domains, suggesting a functional conservation based upon a shared property, possibly a direct interaction with the MT lattice (Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: One of the two structured domains of DCX binds to MTs at the junction of four α/β-tubulin dimers.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) investigations of the DCX–MT interaction reveal that one of the two structured domain binds to MTs at the junction of four α/β-tubulin dimers, stabilizing the longitudinal protofilament and its lateral contacts (Fourniol et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX binding at the junction stabilizes the longitudinal protofilament and its lateral contacts.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) investigations of the DCX–MT interaction reveal that one of the two structured domain binds to MTs at the junction of four α/β-tubulin dimers, stabilizing the longitudinal protofilament and its lateral contacts (Fourniol et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There is uncertainty over the identification of the actual interacting DC domain with the MT lattice.
source: Given the modest resolution of the cryo-EM maps and the structural similarity of DC domains, there is still some uncertainty over the identification of the actual interacting DC domain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a motivation for the study.

claim: NDC was designated as the primary contact at the junction.
source: NDC was designated as the primary contact at the junction, but evidence also suggests that CDC could occupy this site (Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Evidence suggests that CDC could occupy the primary binding site at the junction.
source: NDC was designated as the primary contact at the junction, but evidence also suggests that CDC could occupy this site (Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX has a propensity to dimerize in vitro.
source: The binding mode is clouded further by observations that DCX has a propensity to dimerize in vitro (Caspi et al., 2000), although analytical ultracentrifugation showed that isolated DCX is monomeric even at relatively high concentrations (Moores et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Isolated DCX is monomeric even at relatively high concentrations.
source: The binding mode is clouded further by observations that DCX has a propensity to dimerize in vitro (Caspi et al., 2000), although analytical ultracentrifugation showed that isolated DCX is monomeric even at relatively high concentrations (Moores et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CDC may adopt an open conformation, allowing it to dimerize through a 'domain swapping' event in some MT-assisted fashion.
source: However, CDC may adopt an open conformation, allowing it to dimerize through a 'domain swapping' event in some MT-assisted fashion (Rufer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX interacts with the MT through the CDC domain first, then transitions to an NDC–MT-binding mode in the fully assembled MT lattice.
source: A recent study describes a dynamic interaction model in which DCX interacts with the MT through the CDC domain first, then transitions to an NDC–MT-binding mode in the fully assembled MT lattice (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX manifests a higher affinity to MT ends compared to the MT lattice.
source: For example, DCX manifests a higher affinity to MT ends compared to the MT lattice (Bechstedt et al., 2014) and appears sensitive to MT lateral curvature (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012) and longitudinal curvature (Bechstedt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX appears sensitive to MT lateral curvature.
source: For example, DCX manifests a higher affinity to MT ends compared to the MT lattice (Bechstedt et al., 2014) and appears sensitive to MT lateral curvature (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012) and longitudinal curvature (Bechstedt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX appears sensitive to MT longitudinal curvature.
source: For example, DCX manifests a higher affinity to MT ends compared to the MT lattice (Bechstedt et al., 2014) and appears sensitive to MT lateral curvature (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012) and longitudinal curvature (Bechstedt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DCX binding is strongly cooperative.
source: These observations are difficult to explain through a simple binding mode, particularly given that binding is strongly cooperative and significantly reduces the rate of DCX–MT dissociation (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: DCX binding significantly reduces the rate of DCX–MT dissociation.
source: These observations are difficult to explain through a simple binding mode, particularly given that binding is strongly cooperative and significantly reduces the rate of DCX–MT dissociation (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The study generated a dense set of 362 unique crosslinks between DCX and MT.
source: When applied to the saturated DCX–MT state, the method generated a dense set of 362 unique crosslinks, well distributed among the domains and subunits (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), including 124 interprotein crosslinks between DCX and α/β-tubulin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crosslinking data.

claim: 124 interprotein crosslinks were identified between DCX and α/β-tubulin.
source: When applied to the saturated DCX–MT state, the method generated a dense set of 362 unique crosslinks, well distributed among the domains and subunits (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), including 124 interprotein crosslinks between DCX and α/β-tubulin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crosslinking data.

claim: Adding DCX to purified α/β tubulin induced MT polymerization.
source: In a turbidity assay, adding DCX to purified α/β tubulin-induced MT polymerization, consistent with previous reports (Taylor et al., 2000; Horesh et al., 1999; Moores et al., 2006; Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DCX activity confirmation.

claim: The effect of DCX on MT polymerization saturates at 10–20 µM DCX.
source: The effect saturates at 10–20 µM DCX, in line with previous claims of a 1:1 binding ratio (DCX:α/β-tubulin) (Moores et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DCX activity confirmation.

claim: A pelleting assay confirmed a 1:1 stoichiometry of DCX to α/β-tubulin.
source: A pelleting assay confirmed a 1:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DCX activity confirmation.

claim: MT lengths decrease with increasing DCX concentration.
source: Finally, using a fluorescence image analysis, we observed MT lengths decrease with increasing DCX concentration, confirming a role in MT nucleation (Moores et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DCX activity confirmation.

claim: There were no signs of extensive MT bundling in the presence of DCX.
source: There were no signs of extensive MT bundling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the DCX activity confirmation.

claim: More than 80% of the inter-DCX crosslinks identified involve the CDC domain and the C-tail.
source: Interestingly, >80% of the inter-DCX crosslinks identified involve the CDC domain and the C-tail, which indicates that DCX self-associates on the MT lattice through its C-terminal regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DCX self-association.

claim: DCX self-associates on the MT lattice through its C-terminal regions.
source: Interestingly, >80% of the inter-DCX crosslinks identified involve the CDC domain and the C-tail, which indicates that DCX self-associates on the MT lattice through its C-terminal regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the crosslinking data.

claim: DCX self-association is a MT-dependent phenomenon.
source: We found that only under extreme cases (i.e., DCX denaturation, refolding, and concentrating) could we induce a small amount of interprotein crosslinking, and only at two sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Thus, DCX self-association is a MT-dependent phenomenon, consistent with previous reports (Moores et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on isotopic labeling experiments.

claim: 32 unique intra-DCX crosslink sites were obtained.
source: In total, we obtained 32 unique intra-DCX crosslink sites, 5 unique inter-DCX crosslink sites as well as 45 unique crosslink sites in the mixed group, both inter-DCX and intra-DCX (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crosslinking data.

claim: 5 unique inter-DCX crosslink sites were obtained.
source: In total, we obtained 32 unique intra-DCX crosslink sites, 5 unique inter-DCX crosslink sites as well as 45 unique crosslink sites in the mixed group, both inter-DCX and intra-DCX (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crosslinking data.

claim: 45 unique crosslink sites in the mixed group (both inter-DCX and intra-DCX) were obtained.
source: In total, we obtained 32 unique intra-DCX crosslink sites, 5 unique inter-DCX crosslink sites as well as 45 unique crosslink sites in the mixed group, both inter-DCX and intra-DCX (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crosslinking data.

claim: The top cluster for NDC–MT modeling contained 48% of all models with a cluster precision of 23.4 Å.
source: For NDC–MT, the top cluster contained 48% of all models (cluster precision of 23.4 Å) and identified a site at the junction of the four tubulin dimers resembling the site identified by cryo-EM, albeit with a slightly altered orientation (Figure 4A, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The top cluster for NDC–MT modeling identified a site at the junction of the four tubulin dimers resembling the site identified by cryo-EM.
source: For NDC–MT, the top cluster contained 48% of all models (cluster precision of 23.4 Å) and identified a site at the junction of the four tubulin dimers resembling the site identified by cryo-EM, albeit with a slightly altered orientation (Figure 4A, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The most accurate NDC–MT models had the highest crosslink utilization rate.
source: The most accurate models, as measured by RMSD from the expected site also had the highest crosslink utilization rate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The top cluster for CDC–MT modeling contained 50% of the individual models with a cluster precision of 27.0 Å.
source: The top cluster for CDC–MT contained 50% of the individual models (cluster precision 27.0 Å) and identified a different location, on the interprotofilament junction of two α-tubulin subunits (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The top cluster for CDC–MT modeling identified a location on the interprotofilament junction of two α-tubulin subunits.
source: The top cluster for CDC–MT contained 50% of the individual models (cluster precision 27.0 Å) and identified a different location, on the interprotofilament junction of two α-tubulin subunits (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The addition of EM data to NDC–MT modeling returned the same binding site with 80% of all models in a single distinct cluster with a cluster precision of 6.0 Å.
source: The addition of the EM data to the integrative modeling input, not surprisingly, returned the same binding site for NDC–MT (Figure 4C). A single distinct cluster was generated that contained 80% of all models (with a cluster precision 6.0 Å) and it corrected the orientation of the domain (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The addition of EM data forced the relocation of CDC to the major binding site, with 58% of all models clustered with a precision of 5.9 Å, but the crosslink utilization rate dropped considerably.
source: Conversely, the addition of the EM data forced the relocation of CDC to the major binding site, well removed from the one generated by crosslinking alone. Although 58% of all models clustered with a precision 5.9 Å, the crosslink utilization rate dropped considerably (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the integrative modeling results.

claim: The high congruency between crosslinking and cryo-EM data confirms the location of NDC at the junction.
source: Taken together, the high congruency between crosslinking and cryo-EM data confirms the location of NDC at the junction, whereas the variable localization of the CDC and a weaker restraint set suggests, at best, a secondary binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the modeling data.

claim: The variable localization of the CDC and a weaker restraint set suggests, at best, a secondary binding site for CDC.
source: Taken together, the high congruency between crosslinking and cryo-EM data confirms the location of NDC at the junction, whereas the variable localization of the CDC and a weaker restraint set suggests, at best, a secondary binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the modeling data.

claim: In all modeling scenarios for dimeric DCX, major clusters of solutions were obtained (>98% of models) with a cluster precision of 21–25 Å.
source: In all modeling scenarios, we obtained major clusters of solutions (>98% of models) with a cluster precision of 21–25 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2), each capable of supporting both globular and domain-swapped modes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the dimeric DCX modeling.

claim: An analysis of the overall fit to all DCX–DCX crosslinks shows a weak preference for the domain-swapped conformation.
source: An analysis of the overall fit to all DCX–DCX crosslinks shows a weak preference for the latter (Figure 5B), but we cannot discriminate with high confidence based on utilization rates alone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the dimeric DCX modeling.

claim: An inspection of the centroid model for the main cluster of solutions shows a head-to-tail conformation with strong similarity to the domain-swapped structure.
source: However, an inspection of the centroid model for the main cluster of solutions shows a head-to-tail conformation with strong similarity to the domain-swapped structure (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the dimeric DCX modeling.

claim: There appears a preference for the open conformation through a domain swapping event in the CDC.
source: Taken together, there appears a preference for the open conformation through a domain swapping event in the CDC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the modeling data.

claim: No preferred orientation for the DCX dimer on the lattice could be detected based on crosslink usage.
source: We could detect no preferred orientation for the DCX dimer on the lattice, based on crosslink usage. The distribution of crosslinks shows they accommodate all the orientations equally well (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the full DCX–MT modeling.

claim: The dispersion of crosslink satisfaction suggests that an underlying heterogeneity in lattice engagement is possible.
source: This dispersion suggests that an underlying heterogeneity in lattice engagement is possible.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: In all orientations, regardless of the orientation, the tails are located distal to the lattice and adopt an averaged orientation perpendicular to the long axis of the dimer.
source: In all cases, regardless of the orientation, the tails are located distal to the lattice and adopt an averaged orientation perpendicular to the long axis of the dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the density maps of the ensemble of models.

claim: Removal of the C-tail led to a slight reduction in correlation between mCherry and GFP signals.
source: Our data demonstrate that removal of the C-tail led to a slight reduction in correlation between mCherry and GFP signals, as confirmed by a two-way analysis of variance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cooperativity assay.

claim: The C-tail contributes slightly to cooperativity between neighboring DCX molecules on the MT.
source: In other words, the C-tail contributes slightly to cooperativity between neighboring DCX molecules on the MT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the cooperativity assay.

claim: The function of DCX in MT regulation and brain development is dependent on the full-length protein.
source: The function of DCX in MT regulation and brain development is dependent on the full-length protein and we propose that this function is strongly dependent upon its self-association.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: DCX function is strongly dependent upon its self-association.
source: The function of DCX in MT regulation and brain development is dependent on the full-length protein and we propose that this function is strongly dependent upon its self-association.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal based on the findings.

claim: A lattice-induced dimerization event is the dominant state at the stoichiometry explored in this study.
source: Based on the data-directed models that we generated in this study and the high fraction of crosslinking data that was satisfied, a lattice-induced dimerization event is the dominant state at the stoichiometry we explored.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The association could adopt a variety of orientations on the stabilized MT lattice.
source: However, the association could adopt a variety of orientations on the stabilized MT lattice, consistent with an initial contact complex that involves just a monomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The flexibility of the interdomain region could support the precession of the monomer, allowing it to capture a suitably positioned additional monomer.
source: That is, the flexibility of the interdomain region could support the precession of the monomer, allowing it to capture a suitably positioned additional monomer (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: A primary binding mode involving the CDC at the junctional sites is unlikely in the MT polymerization state that was studied.
source: A primary binding mode involving the CDC at the junctional sites is unlikely in the MT polymerization state that was studied here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: An earlier observation highlighted strong binding cooperativity, revealing a Hill coefficient approaching 3 for DCX binding to 13-protofilament MTs.
source: An earlier observation highlighted strong binding cooperativity, revealing a Hill coefficient approaching 3 for DCX binding to 13-protofilament MTs (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The remarkable degree of cooperativity suggests that associations beyond dimeric are indeed possible and could involve the long C-tails.
source: This remarkable degree of cooperativity suggests that associations beyond dimeric are indeed possible and could involve the long C-tails.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the cooperativity data.

claim: The clinical truncation at R303, removing most of the tail, leads to a slight drop in cooperative binding.
source: Our observation that the clinical truncation at R303, removing most of the tail, leads to a slight drop in cooperative binding suggests the tail has only a minor role in maintaining associations between DCX molecules on the MT lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the cooperativity assay results.

claim: The tail has only a minor role in maintaining associations between DCX molecules on the MT lattice.
source: Our observation that the clinical truncation at R303, removing most of the tail, leads to a slight drop in cooperative binding suggests the tail has only a minor role in maintaining associations between DCX molecules on the MT lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the cooperativity assay results.

claim: The tail is not the sole source of cooperativity, as mutations in the structured CDC itself lead to rapid dissociation from the lattice.
source: The tail is not the sole source of cooperativity, as mutations in the structured CDC itself lead to rapid dissociation from the lattice (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Disease specific mutations in both CDC and C-tail regions provide strong evidence for the functional significance of lattice-driven self-association.
source: Disease specific mutations in both of these regions provide strong evidence for the functional significance of lattice-driven self-association.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the mutation data.

claim: Crystallographic evidence suggests that the CDC can dimerize under mildly denaturing conditions.
source: Crystallographic evidence suggests that the CDC can dimerize under mildly denaturing conditions (Rufer et al., 2018) whereas cryo-EM data indicate that both NDC and CDC can bind to the lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Cryo-EM data indicate that both NDC and CDC can bind to the lattice.
source: Crystallographic evidence suggests that the CDC can dimerize under mildly denaturing conditions (Rufer et al., 2018) whereas cryo-EM data indicate that both NDC and CDC can bind to the lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referencing prior cryo-EM studies.

claim: A recent cryo-EM study confirms that the CDC domain participates in MT nucleation at the junctional site but as the lattice grows, the sites become mostly occupied with NDC domains.
source: A recent cryo-EM study by the Moores lab confirms that the CDC domain participates in MT nucleation at the junctional site but as the lattice grows, the sites become mostly occupied with NDC domains (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Interactions between NDC and the MT lattice induce an opening of the CDC, leading to a binding event that favors the published crystallographic structure of the dimerized CDC.
source: We propose a model where interactions between NDC and the MT lattice induce an opening of the CDC, leading to a binding event that favors the published crystallographic structure of the dimerized CDC (Rufer et al., 2018; Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed model.

claim: The dimerization must be induced as it does not exist in solution without the MT interaction.
source: The dimerization must be induced as it does not exist in solution without the MT interaction (Moores et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The conformational state of the CDC in the lattice-bound form is quite distinct from the X-ray structure of the free domain.
source: The cryo-EM data seem to support this, as the conformational state of the CDC in the lattice-bound form is quite distinct from the X-ray structure of the free domain (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Induced dimerization provides an explanation for the transition from an early CDC–MT interaction to an NDC–MT interaction.
source: Induced dimerization provides an explanation for the transition from an early CDC–MT interaction to an NDC–MT interaction (Manka and Moores, 2020; Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: CDC participates in nucleating MT growth when centrosomal γTURC complexes are not available, as is the case in the distal ends of migrating neurons.
source: It was proposed that CDC participates in nucleating MT growth when centrosomal γTURC complexes are not available, as is the case in the distal ends of migrating neurons (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The deformable CDC domain creates junctional sites that may be somewhat different than the sites in the mature MT lattice because of the curved nature of the nucleated tubulin oligomers.
source: The deformable CDC domain creates junctional sites that may be somewhat different than the sites in the mature MT lattice because of the curved nature of the nucleated tubulin oligomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: As the lattice fully assembles and regular junctional sites are formed, the more rigid NDC domain can now bind.
source: As the lattice fully assembles and regular junctional sites are formed, the more rigid NDC domain can now bind.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed model.

claim: Neither of the two structured domains bind to the lattice particularly strongly on their own.
source: It is important to note that neither of the two structured domains bind to the lattice particularly strongly on their own, thus a transition to NDC binding could readily occur upon lattice maturation (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Induced unfolding of CDC followed by its capture in a dimeric state would explain how DCX binds to the lattice so avidly.
source: Induced unfolding of CDC followed by its capture in a dimeric state would explain how DCX binds to the lattice so avidly and such an association would certainly prevent CDC from rebinding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: Dimerization would stabilize the MT lattice and offer a compelling reason for favoring MTs with a well-defined number of protofilaments.
source: At the same time, dimerization would stabilize the MT lattice and offer a compelling reason for favoring MTs with a well-defined number of protofilaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: The more rigid NDC coupled with its larger footprint on the lattice is better positioned than the CDC to set the angle of curvature.
source: That is, the more rigid NDC coupled with its larger footprint on the lattice (Manka and Moores, 2020) is better positioned than the CDC to set the angle of curvature, and dimerization increases the local concentrations of these domains on the lattice through avidity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A double NDC construct induces much more MT bundling than the WT.
source: A double NDC construct induces much more MT bundling than the WT (Manka and Moores, 2020), very likely through cross-lattice interactions, suggesting that dimerization minimizes these interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Dimerization minimizes cross-lattice interactions that lead to bundling.
source: A double NDC construct induces much more MT bundling than the WT (Manka and Moores, 2020), very likely through cross-lattice interactions, suggesting that dimerization minimizes these interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the bundling observation.

claim: Mutations in the NDC could lead to reduced binding.
source: Mutations in the NDC could certainly lead to reduced binding (Manka and Moores, 2020), but the mutations in the CDC region would more likely interfere with dimerization, reduce the avidity of DCX on the lattice, and diminish MT stabilization overall (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutations in the CDC region would more likely interfere with dimerization, reduce the avidity of DCX on the lattice, and diminish MT stabilization overall.
source: Mutations in the NDC could certainly lead to reduced binding (Manka and Moores, 2020), but the mutations in the CDC region would more likely interfere with dimerization, reduce the avidity of DCX on the lattice, and diminish MT stabilization overall (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Removing the C-tail reduces the preference for 13-protofilament MTs.
source: Removing the C-tail reduces the preference for 13-protofilament MTs (Moores et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Removing the C-tail slightly increases DCX affinity to MTs.
source: Although its removal slightly increases DCX affinity to MTs, it also reduces the rate of DCX accumulation on the lattice (Moslehi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Removing the C-tail reduces the rate of DCX accumulation on the lattice.
source: Although its removal slightly increases DCX affinity to MTs, it also reduces the rate of DCX accumulation on the lattice (Moslehi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The depth of crosslinking observed in the C-tail region suggests an induced structure.
source: The depth of crosslinking we observed in this region suggests an induced structure, perhaps a coiled-coil as observed with other dimerized MAPs (Slep et al., 2005; Kon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the crosslinking data.

claim: DeepCoil shows a very low probability of a coiled-coil domain in the C-tail.
source: However, DeepCoil (Ludwiczak et al., 2019) shows a very low probability of such a domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A more extensive multi-DCX network backed by a dynamically interacting set of C-tails would contribute to the high cooperativity of binding and help stabilize DCX on the lattice.
source: A more extensive multi-DCX network backed by a dynamically interacting set of C-tails would contribute to the high cooperativity of binding and help stabilize DCX on the lattice (see insets in Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Phosphorylation of S297 by Cdk5 reduces DCX affinity to MTs in cultured neurons.
source: For example, phosphorylation of S297 by Cdk5 reduces DCX affinity to MTs in cultured neurons and any mutations (phosphomimics or dephosphomimics) similarly reduce affinity and alter neuronal migration patterns (Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Any mutations at S297 (phosphomimics or dephosphomimics) similarly reduce affinity and alter neuronal migration patterns.
source: For example, phosphorylation of S297 by Cdk5 reduces DCX affinity to MTs in cultured neurons and any mutations (phosphomimics or dephosphomimics) similarly reduce affinity and alter neuronal migration patterns (Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Spinophilin-induced dephosphorylation of S297 by PP1 causes an increase MT bundling in the axonal shaft of neurons.
source: Conversely, spinophilin-induced dephosphorylation of S297 by PP1 causes an increase MT bundling in the axonal shaft of neurons (Bielas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Higher-order self-association and its regulation are important to DCX function on the MT lattice.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that higher-order self-association and its regulation are important to DCX function on the MT lattice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the phosphorylation data.

claim: DCX recognizes a specific tubulin spacing in the lattice, favoring longitudinal curvatures that result in shorter interdimer distances.
source: DCX recognizes a specific tubulin spacing in the lattice, favoring longitudinal curvatures that result in shorter interdimer distances (Ettinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Missense mutations in the CDC region (and not NDC) disrupt the longitudinal curvature detection properties of DCX.
source: Missense mutations in the CDC region (and not NDC) disrupt the longitudinal curvature detection properties of DCX, but this could influence dimerization as well.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: A lateral interaction seems the most likely given the orientation of the NDC–CDC linker in cryo-EM models.
source: Our integrative modeling is not sufficiently precise to identify a dominant orientation (if one truly exists), but a lateral interaction seems the most likely given the orientation of the NDC–CDC linker in cryo-EM models (Manka and Moores, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A dimer with an ability to engage the lattice in a lateral manner could reinforce a preference for a 13-protofilament lattice, if the 'bite length' of the dimer is complementary to protofilament spacing.
source: A dimer with an ability to engage the lattice in a lateral manner could reinforce a preference for a 13-protofilament lattice, if the 'bite length' of the dimer is complementary to protofilament spacing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: The success of this integrative modeling technique relies heavily upon an improved crosslinking methodology that samples the equilibrated state more faithfully.
source: Finally, the success of this integrative modeling technique relies heavily upon an improved crosslinking methodology that samples the equilibrated state more faithfully (Ziemianowicz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The presence of nominally disordered regions in MAPs like DCX renders proteins prone to 'kinetic trapping' on the lattice.
source: The presence of nominally disordered regions in MAPs like DCX renders proteins prone to 'kinetic trapping' on the lattice, where conventional long-lived crosslinking reagents can trap interactions in non-native states.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for the improved methodology.

claim: The outcome of the integrative modeling using conventional crosslinking chemistries (DSS and EDC) was poor, both in terms of the percent crosslink satisfaction (<50%) and the location of the primary binding site.
source: We conducted a modeling analysis of the DCX–MT interaction using typical DSS (disuccinimidyl suberate) and EDC(1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide) crosslinkers and while the data are abundant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), the outcome of the integrative modeling using conventional crosslinking chemistries was poor, both in terms of the percent crosslink satisfaction (<50%) and the location of the primary binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the comparison with conventional crosslinkers.

claim: The full modeling exercise with DSS and EDC data provided no interpretable results.
source: The full modeling exercise with these data provided no interpretable results.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the comparison with conventional crosslinkers.
